 Early voting initiatives gave JOCO voters opportunities to cast their ballot early
 To make voting accessible to voters in Johnson County, the auditor’s office provided many early voting opportunities. 
 Elizabeth Connor , News Reporter 
 • 
 November 17, 2026 
 John Charlson ‘I voted’ stickers are seen inside Lemme Elementary School on Election Day in Iowa City on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Lemme Elementary serves as Iowa City’s precinct 1 polling location. The Iowa ballot for the 2026 Midterm Elections contains open races for governor and U.S. Senate. 
 When thinking of elections, most people go to the polls on the first Tuesday of November and wait in line to cast their ballots. However, in Johnson County some people chose to cast their ballot early and the auditor’s office wanted to increase this number. 
 In the 19 days leading up to Nov. 3, 36,473 people cast a ballot either by mail or early voting in Johnson County. That’s 47 percent of the 77,575 people who voted in this year’s midterm election.  
 In 2022, only 40 percent of voters voted early, so early voting increased significantly from 2022 to 2026.  
 However, these numbers didn’t appear out of thin air. Instead, they are the result of local initiatives from the Johnson County Auditor’s Office to get voters to the polls before Election Day.  
 Julie Persons, the JoCo auditor, said every eligible voter in the county should have an easy time getting to the polls, even if her office had more work to do.  
 “I didn’t want anyone in Johnson County to say, ‘I didn’t have a chance to vote,’” Persons said. “That’s why we do so much early voting.”  
 To do this, she and her staff spearheaded myriad initiatives to bolster early voting in Johnson County.  
 First, they set up 10 early voting satellite locations around the county. These locations could be anywhere in the county, from libraries in Coralville to the Iowa Memorial Union. These locations were specifically chosen because of their convenience and popularity.  
 In general, Persons asked one question when thinking about satellite locations: “What do Johnson County voters want?” 
 Voters could come into any of those locations during their hours and vote, no matter what precinct they lived in. In contrast, voting on Election Day only allows for voters to cast a ballot at their specific polling location.  
 In total, there were 93 hours of satellite voting time available to Johnson County voters starting Oct. 14.  
 However, opening those locations wasn’t smooth sailing. Because of state law, auditors can’t decide to plop a satellite location wherever they think would be best. Instead, the voters themselves must petition, and obtain 100 signatures, for each location.  
 Nonetheless, Persons was able to coordinate with local organizations, such as Indivisible Iowa Johnson County, to garner enough signatures for each location. 
 Indivisible Iowa Johnson County worked with the auditor’s office to open a satellite location at Dream City, which is just south of Highway 6. For Jim Jacobson, a member of Indivisible Iowa JoCo, recent federal attempts to limit voter registration made early voting more crucial than ever.  
 “We were saying, ‘If they’re going to do that, then we have to make sure that people get out to vote, and get out to vote early,’” Jacobson said.  
 Jacobson was amazed at the efforts to encourage early voting in Johnson County and praised everyone involved.  
 “It had to be done by people on the ground by organizations like Indivisible and No Kings and people like Julie Persons promoting early voting. It took a lot of people,” Jacobson said.  
 Isabella Tisdale 
 Ultimately, 215 people voted at Dream City, a significant increase from previous elections. 
 Other than satellite locations, the auditor’s office kept its office open for early voters as often as possible. By state code, the auditor’s office is required to have early voting on weekdays — usually for six hours a day and typically during normal business hours — and the Saturday before the election.  
 Anything beyond those times is not required.  
 But Persons and her staff decided to stay open as much as possible. Their weekday early voting hours were from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. from Oct. 14 to Nov. 2. Additionally, they had three days of “Voting After Dark,” where the office stayed open until 8 p.m.  
 According to the auditor’s office, 770 people voted after 5 p.m., proving to Persons and her staff that the extra hours were worth it.  
 Finally, the office had several days of weekend voting on Oct. 24, 25, 31, and Nov. 1, which is three extra days from what’s required by code.  
 In addition to extra hours and locations, the office also worked hard to communicate the correct information to voters via outreach initiatives.  
 Kenzie Northup, the outreach officer for the auditor’s office, aimed to get information out to voters in a variety of ways. She posted on social media and sent out several mailers to voters to make sure they had the information they needed.  
 “It’s really a goal and a mission of our office to equip as many people as we can with the correct information so that then they can go to their channels and give the information to the people who are asking them where to vote, how to vote, and how to make a plan to vote,” Northup said.  
 To Northup, early voting opportunities are critical to making sure everyone gets to vote.  
 “You never know what’s going to happen on election day,” she said. “Something could come up and then you’re going to be out of luck.”
